body: I believe this only applies if you are using HTML4x.  If you are using XHTML or HTML 5 this shouldn't be the case.

author: Fed
body:
I was adding my scripts to a SquareSpace version 5 site, which uses the "XHTML 1.0 Strict" doctype, and was seeing the problem. Perhaps on a page with an HTML5 doctype it wouldn't be a problem, though I didn't test that scenario.

For backward compatibility--or to fail gracefully--I'll still continue to use the non-atomic version of the script tag.

author: Fed
body: UPDATE: Out of curiosity, I just tested this and could not get self-closing script tags to work. Maybe I was doing something wrong, but it didn't seem to matter what doctype I used. Whenever I didn't add a closing script tag, my Javascript files did not load.

author: Alex
body:
So, this is all a bit odd. I too did several tests and found that what you say is the case. Self-closing tags don't work in either XHTML Transitional, Strict, or HTML5. The W3C validator is happy to pass either the separate closing or self-closing variants in XHTML, however in HTML5 validation it actually produces an error:

Self-closing syntax (/>) used on a non-void HTML element. Ignoring the slash and treating as a start tag.

According to the XHTML and HTML5 specs (your link references the HTML4 spec), either is actually valid, but it just happens that the major browser implementations require a separate close tag. This is unfortunately an example of another place in web programming where you CAN'T code to the spec, you have to code to the implementations.
